https://www.politico.eu/article/volodymy.text: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday flatly rejected a call by his former defense chief to send the country to the ballot box. “I believe that during a war like this, elections in general carry significant risks,” Zelenskyy told journalists — including POLITICO — behind closed doors. A vote “right now would be a tsunami for the state, one that would tear Ukraine apart,” the Ukrainian president said. He added that his strategy is to lead his people “to the end of the war and preserve an independent and sovereign state.” Advertisement Advertisement His remarks come after former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov — ousted from his government role in July following a controversial reshuffle — called for elections earlier this week . Organizing a vote “safely, legitimately, and democratically” in Ukraine, with the participation of soldiers on the front line and citizens who fled to other countries to escape the war, requires “specific conditions,” Zelenskyy continued. That’s “impossible under the current conditions, when Putin refuses to consider any options for a ceasefire,” he argued. Fedorov has emerged as a rival to the current president. In a video address Tuesday, he argued that “people cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made.” But his appeal has been criticized by both Zelenskyy allies and opposition members: Critics said elections — which are suspended under Ukraine’s martial law, in place since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022 — would only strengthen the Kremlin’s position and sow division. Fedorov seems undeterred and doubled down in comments to the BBC on Sunday , saying he has a “moral right” to raise the topic of elections. “If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: A pilot from Ukraine’s 413 Raid drone regiment waiting to launch mid-range attack drones in eastern Ukraine. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian A conflict that began with tanks and then artillery is now pivoting around a new generation of drones focused on military, industrial, economic and civilian targets By Dan Sabbagh in eastern Ukraine. With photographs by Julia Kochetova Thu 24 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google F inally, in the dead of night, the threat above has passed. The rain has eased and the Ukrainian drones are ready, prepared by a ground crew shrouded in hard-to-detect green and red lights. A small succession of Ukrainian Fire Point FP-2 craft, miniature monoplanes with a 6-metre wingspan and more than 100kg of explosive, line up for an attack mission into occupied Luhansk, over 200 miles away. The drone’s main piston engine is a familiar scooter’s buzz, but its launch booster is something else. The jet sound reverberates, almost painfully. A burst of fire lurches into the distance, the last of which signifies it is time for Ukraine’s 413 Raid drone regiment to pack and go. View image in fullscreen The launch of an FP-2 drone during the mission into occupied Luhansk It is a scene that is now played out nightly by dozens of Ukrainian crews, reflecting a fast-changing conflict that began with tanks, then artillery, but is now pivoting beyond a first generation of drones. Death and destruction are delivered by new weapons in growing volumes, hundreds of miles beyond the frontline, and at targets that are military, industrial and economic but that affect civilians too. But just as Ukraine has developed its drone and missile capability to almost match Russia’s – after its cities were subject at times to hundreds of drone strikes a day – Moscow has transformed its drone arsenal with a jet-powered revolution. The balance of power remains uncertain. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Pilots of the 413 Raid drone regiment preparing an FP-2 for launch Raid is a specialist drone unit, created two years ago, and has been operating Ukrainian-designed and -built FP-2 attack drones since last autumn, according to Skipper, a former corporate IT worker with a master’s in computer science who is now one of its commanders. If, he says, there was only one crew that could run two missions a week when they started, today he says “we can do 10 times more, or even more”. Speaking in a car as the rain pelts down, Skipper cautions there is “a flipside” when asked if long-distance wars are easier to fight because nobody has to be killed visibly. “They can do it as well,” he says – Raid’s crew are targets too. “Maybe you don’t see the enemy with your own eyes, but still it’s a very dangerous game,” he adds. The FP-2 was only first publicly acknowledged by Ukraine last September. It is designed to attack hardened targets at a mid-range, to disrupt Russian logistics to the frontline. The success of Raid and others engaged in mid-strike bombing has helped grind the pace of the invaders’ advance to a near halt. Russia gained a modest 90 square kilometres of Ukraine in August, compared with 505 sq km a year earlier, and western officials estimate it is losing 6,000 more soldiers a month than it can recruit. Ukrainian drones and missiles chart In Ukraine’s sprawling military, the specialist drone units of the Unmanned System Forces, including Raid regiment, work and overlap with army units working closer to the frontline and special forces. A major attack, such as the attack that disabled the Moscow refinery about 300 miles from the border on 20 September, involves several working at once. A long-range attack could involve launching up to 300 drones, though the target is to be able to launch 1,000 a night, in what soldiers describe as an “orchestra”, where cheap drones identify an air corridor towards the final target. View image in fullscreen An employee walks past a plume of smoke rising from a fire at the Russian e-commerce firm Wildberries’ logistics complex near the town of Podolsk, outside Moscow, on 16 August. Photograph: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images The long-range, $75,000 FP-1 , sister to the FP-2, has been used to repeatedly attack warehouses, refineries and other military-economic sites at a depth of 1,800 miles inside Russia, causing the country’s crude oil production to fall by 7.7% in a year, according to figures from the International Energy Agency, and interest rates to remain at 14%. “Both sides are getting better at translating deep strikes into economic effects,” says Sidharth Kaushal, of the Royal United Services Institute. View image in fullscreen A refinery burning in Moscow after Ukrainian drones strikes, 21 September. Photograph: EyePress News/Shutterstock Mission planning is rarely shown, but a short-range drone unit operating in the eastern Donetsk front – Unit 17, Special Operations Centre – is happy to show their war work from their dacha. Znakhar, 33, a software coder before the full Russian invasion, is one of a squad of English-speaking men in their early 30s. During the day, he clicks on fresh, static targets – artillery, electronic jamming systems – that have been added to a common system from western satellites or Ukrainian reconnaissance drones, studying their pictures for extra information. View image in fullscreen Pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre, posing for a portrait next to a Sych mid-strike drone View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen The temporary base of pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre. Right: the ‘drop bombs’ Unit 17 used for middle strikes At night, the crew use a $25,000 Sych drone, which looks like a large model aeroplane. If the rain holds off, they can fly two to six bombing runs, dozens of miles behind enemy lines. Znakhar, whose call sign means healer or herbalist, draws up an initial flight path in seconds with a few clicks on a map, then adjusts the route to avoid population centres, high ground and known interceptor drone launch sites. What’s changed recently? “More drones,” he says. “Russian drones.” Colleagues such as Ananas, 30, head out at night, taking more precautions than they did when the unit started drone work two years ago, preparing launches underground where once they could work in a field. He studied architecture, then worked as a 3D artist in a video game studio. “I play a lot of video games,” he says, “so I’m good with a gamepad. It’s a big plus because now I’m a pilot.” It’s a narrowing of the gap between fiction and reality. O n the other side, Moscow always has ballistic and cruise missiles available, allowing it to bomb anywhere inside Ukraine since February 2022. It imported delta-winged Shahed drones from Iran in the war’s first year to boost its long-range attack numbers, and developed a family of cheap battlefield drones plus its own version of the Shahed. But since May there has been a notable set of upgrades, allowing Russian forces to strike Ukraine more effectively with fast, jet-engined drones, allied with a new ruthlessness of targeting. View image in fullscreen Firefighters working at the site of a Russian drone strike on Kyiv business centre on 23 September “Russia never stops,” Serhii Beskrestnov, Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser, said during an interview in Kyiv punctuated by an air raid and explosions in the distance. The original Iranian delta wing Shahed (known by Russia as the Geran-2) has been redesigned and a jet engine added. The new Geran-4, with more aerodynamic wings, flies at anywhere from 300km/h (186mph) to 550km/h, while the cigar-shaped Geran-5 is even faster, at closer to 600km/h. It is similar in speed to a new light cruise missile, the Banderol. The prediction is that Russia will make 36,000 jet Shaheds in 2027, a further 10,000 Banderols, plus a similar number of cheap cruise missiles, the Dan-T. All could be used to bomb Ukraine’s strained electricity, heating and water systems this winter. Russian drones and missiles chart The new weapons, whose Telefly engines are made in China, are faster than the Ukrainian interceptors, designed to stop the old piston-engined Shahed Geran-2s. Shahed interception rates, once over 90%, are down to 60% against Russia’s newer models, with predictable results. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen The aftermath of a Russian attack on ammunition storage in Myla village, Kyiv region, in August A mix of jet- and traditional-engined drones made a rare morning attack into the centre of Kyiv on Wednesday, bombing a market near the central railway station and business centre, killing two people and injuring 41. At the end of August, a Geran-4 hit an ammunition dump at Myla, outside Kyiv, killing 38 and destroying homes nearby. Another struck Ukraine’s SBU domestic intelligence agency in the centre of Kyiv, though it may have been controlled in its final phase by a Russian agent on the ground. Food supplies in Kyiv supermarkets are uneven after sustained attacks on warehouses in August; petrol stations in the capital were targeted in early September. View image in fullscreen The aftermath of a Russian Geran-5-type jet-powered drone strike on an Ukrnafta petrol station in the Holosiivskyi district of Kyiv, 15 September. Photograph: Libkos/Getty Images U krainian military propaganda is excellent at highlighting successful missions on social media, but the wider picture of the impact of its drone strikes on Russia is harder to discern. “This spring we had a really nice time and almost every night we could see one, two, three, four systems destroyed,” Skipper says. “Since June, July, they are just hiding.” Other Ukrainian military sources emphasise that Russia has improved its jamming capabilities, and cheap strike drones are simply not as accurate now. In this long-distance war, civilian casualties are climbing. New UN figures show 2,222 killed in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, more than in all of 2025. In August, 368 were killed in Ukraine and a further 113 reported dead in Russia. Warehouses owned by Ukrainian supermarkets, its Nova Poshta postal service and e-commerce groups were hit at least 32 times. Wildberries and Ozon warehouses in Russia were bombed 17 times by Ukraine. View image in fullscreen Firefighters at a warehouse in the Kyiv region after a Russian attack The impact could be harder for Ukraine. “Russia has advantages that Ukraine does not,” says Kaushal. “A more diversified range of long-range weapons, more of an air defence network and more slack as a society, because its people have not faced so much pressure for so long.” Ukraine, meanwhile, faces economic pressure at a time when its war budget is overspent and needs to find £40bn more next year. Yet, though war is escalating as the technology changes, neither side is close to defeat or a crisis. Tests will come if Russia tries to mobilise up to 300,000 men after parliamentary elections – and as Ukraine tries again to refinance and, most urgently, get through the winter. Back in their soldiers’ dacha, Ananas and Znakhar wonder if the war will ever end. “Sometimes I catch this feeling,” Ananas admits, then Znakhar comes in: “We just need to hang on one more day than them.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia Drones (military) Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://thefrontierpost.com/belarus-free.text: Belarus on Wednesday freed 25 political prisoners as the United States lifted sanctions on two of the reclusive country’s companies, US envoy John Coale announced after his latest visit to Minsk. The release on Wednesday marked the culmination of a series of negotiations stretching back more than a year between Coale and Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Those freed include human rights campaigners, political activists, journalists and lawyers. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius, where the freed prisoners were taken, Coale said he expected to return in about a month when he hopes to see “hundreds” freed. The US envoy praised US President Donald Trump on social media, saying his “commitment to direct diplomacy delivers results” and that the administration would continue to “improve US-Belarus relations”. Coale had been tasked by Trump with securing the release of hundreds of people. In March, the government of Belarus released 250 prisoners following a pardon. Lukashenko, in charge of the former Soviet state since 1994, has long been shunned by the West for repressing his opponents and supporting Russia’s war in Ukraine. The releases came a day after Coale promised Lukashenko that US banks would return tens of millions of dollars in ⁠frozen Belarusian assets. The US envoy earlier said that the US would lift sanctions on Lakokraska, a paint and industrial coating manufacturer, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned industrial enterprise that oversees the forestry, pulp and paper sectors. Christian Wigand, the European Union’s lead spokesperson for foreign affairs and security policy, said the 25 prisoners were released as a result of US efforts. “We welcome this step,” he wrote on X. “800+ individuals remain arbitrarily detained in appalling conditions. Belarus’ regime should release all political prisoners, immediately and unconditionally.” Journalists, musicians among those arrested The Belarusian human rights watchdog Viasna, which the government banned after declaring the group an extremist organisation, said many of those released on Wednesday had been sentenced to several years in prison. The organisation named journalist Andrei Alyaksandrau, who had been serving a 14-year term, among those released. Alyaksandrau had been arrested in 2021 for allegedly “financing protest activities” alongside his girlfriend Iryna Zlobina, who was handed a nine-year sentence. Alyaksandrau told Viasna he had lost 30kgs (66 pounds) while in captivity “for the motherland” but was “in a good mood”. He added that he was “very glad that these almost six years are over” and that he hadn’t seen Zlobina – whom he married in a pre-trial detention centre in 2022 – in four years. Alongside Alyaksandrau, three other journalists – Dzmitry Navazhylau, Kiryl Pazniak and Liudmila Chekina – were released and immediately deported to Lithuania. Reporters Without Borders said it was “delighted” by their release but denounced their expulsion. Exiled political opposition leader Svetlana Tsikhanouskaya said she was happy for the relatives of the 25 freed prisoners “who have been waiting for this day”. Her husband, Siarhei Tsikhanouski, was freed last year after spending five years in jail. “Every release requires tremendous effort, and it is clear that [Lukashenko] does not want to release all political prisoners,” she wrote on X, noting that hundreds more remain behind bars. https://universitytimes.ie/2026/10/trini.text: Trinity Journal of Literary Translation Launches Newest Issue: “Rebellion” On Thursday, Oct 1 at 6:30 p.m., Trinity students gathered in the Hist Conversation Room to celebrate the launch of the first issue of volume fifteen of non-profit literary publication Trinity Journal of Literary Translation (JoLT), founded in 2013. The theme of JoLT’s latest edition is “Rebellion,” a sentiment which is alive at the heart of each carefully-translated piece of poetry and prose, from Baudelaire to Machado and beyond. This issue invites readers to “consider interpretations of rebellion through a wide range of literary genres in translation: self-affirmation, resistance to oppression, empowerment of people.” As artfully-dressed students sipped white wine from stemmed glasses, JoLT Editor-in-Chief Jules Nati introduced the issue and invited contributors to read their translated pieces. First, Tyna Szwiec, a postgraduate student who grew up in Poland, read her English- translation of “Do prostego człowieka,” (or “To the Simple Man”) by Julian Tuwim, a poem which challenges propaganda and conveys anti-war sentiments. Szwiec read the piece first in English and again in Polish, bringing new life to the piece with its original linguistic form. Next, Cyril Huziev read from his translation of Russian poet Zinaida Hippius’s “Zametki o chelovechestve,” or “Notes on Humanity,” a convention-breaking piece that explores the “political and social cataclysms” of 20th century Russia, as noted in Huziev’s introduction to the piece. Next, Deputy Editor of JoLT and Polish native Jes Paluchowska read from their translation of the 1939 Polish poem “Runą” by Zbigniew Turek, who wrote under the pseudonym Adam Śreżoga. “When read vertically, it praises Stalin and the Soviet regime, but upon horizontal reading the text reveals itself to be pro-Polish propaganda,” reads Paluchowska’s introduction to the translated work. Each translated piece is printed next to its original form, allowing readers to experience the works in their full configurations. ADVERTISEMENT Over eight different languages are represented in the issue, from Irish to Kazakh to Czech, and many of the translators who read at the launch offered context to the works they translated, drawing from their own cultural knowledge to enrich the experience of reading and listening to the pieces. Published twice yearly, the issues also feature student-produced artwork that enhances the translations with visual manifestations of the issue’s theme. Fourteen of approximately thirty submitted translations were published in this issue, selected by a staff of twelve editors. Editor-in-Chief Jules Nati explained that translation can be a personal and intimate form of understanding a piece of text. “For translations, you think your own voice disappears behind the translations, but it’s actually not true,” Nati said. “With every word chosen, you can also see how the person translating is feeling.” For those interested in trying their hand at translating a favorite work, JoLT is currently accepting submissions for the next issue of their fifteenth volume, centered around the theme of “Mysticism.” Submissions close Sunday, October 25 and can be sent to trinityjolt@gmail.com. Submissions are also open for visual art related to the theme of mysticism. The newest issue can be read virtually on JoLT’s website.
